extracted.intended_audience: students, citizens, policymakers, and advocates interested in free speech, individual liberty, and public discussion
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical guidance on when opinions and actions should be permitted, the moral norms of public discussion, and the value of individuality and experimental modes of life; explains limits (harm, incitement), virtues of contestation, and proper manners of advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not silence opinions because they may be true
rubrics_metrics.description: "First, if any opinion is compelled to silence, that opinion may, for aught we can certainly know, be true. To deny this is to assume our own infallibility."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silencing an opinion risks suppressing truth; therefore opinions should be permitted unless there is clear reason otherwise. This is a fundamental justification for freedom of opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow expression of opinions that may be erroneous because they often contain partial truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "Though the silenced opinion be an error, it may, and very commonly does, contain a portion of truth; and since the general or prevailing opinion on any subject is rarely or never the whole truth, it is only by the collision of adverse opinions that the remainder of the truth has any chance of being supplied."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even false views can supply elements of truth; contestation helps complete understanding. Encourage hearing opposing views rather than suppressing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even true received opinions must be contested to retain their rational force
rubrics_metrics.description: "Even if the received opinion be not only true, but the whole truth; unless it is suffered to be, and actually is, vigorously and earnestly contested, it will... be held in the manner of a prejudice, with little comprehension or feeling of its rational grounds."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing challenges to dominant doctrines prevents them degenerating into dead dogma; vigorous debate strengthens rather than weakens true doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict expression only when it is a direct instigation to harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions lose immunity when the circumstances of expression "are such as to constitute their expression a positive instigation to some mischievous act." Example: speech accusing corn-dealers of starving the poor may be harmless in print but punishable if delivered to an excited mob before a corn-dealer's house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between mere advocacy and speech that creates immediate risk of harm or incitement; limit the latter. Context (audience, situation) is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual liberty to act on opinions should be allowed so long as one does not harm others (the nuisance/harm limit)
rubrics_metrics.description: "If he refrains from molesting others in what concerns them, and merely acts according to his own inclination and judgment in things which concern himself, ... he should be allowed, without molestation, to carry his opinions into practice at his own cost."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People should be free to experiment with modes of life and to live according to their own judgment unless their actions unjustifiably harm others — the boundary is prevention of harm or making oneself a nuisance.

rubrics_metrics.name: It is impossible to fix clear legal bounds for 'temperate' manner; law should not police ordinary controversial misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: On proposals that free expression be permitted only if 'temperate': "Much might be said on the impossibility of fixing where these supposed bounds are to be placed... the principal offences... are such as it is mostly impossible... to bring home to conviction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because tests of temperateness are subjective and many controversial faults (sophistry, suppression of facts) are hard to prove legally, reliance on law to police manners of debate is inappropriate; encourage moral/societal remedies instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sophistical argument, suppression or misrepresentation of facts — these are the gravest offences in debate
rubrics_metrics.description: The gravest offences are "to argue sophistically, to suppress facts or arguments, to misstate the elements of the case, or misrepresent the opposite opinion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such practices undermine truth-seeking; they merit severe censure in public opinion though are often committed in good faith and are difficult to punish legally. Strive for honesty and completeness in argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemn personal calumny and stigmatization of opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: "The worst offence... is to stigmatize those who hold the contrary opinion as bad and immoral men. To calumny of this sort, those who hold any unpopular opinion are peculiarly exposed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal attacks and calumny disproportionately harm minorities and deter dissent; public opinion should especially condemn stigmatizing opponents rather than tolerate it when employed against the less powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of language is strategically necessary for unpopular opinions to be heard
rubrics_metrics.description: "In general, opinions contrary to those commonly received can only obtain a hearing by studied moderation of language, and the most cautious avoidance of unnecessary offence... without losing ground."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minority advocates should exercise restraint and avoid unnecessary offence to gain a hearing; while dominant voices may use harsher language with less penalty, such vituperation is harmful to fair discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: The proper morality of public discussion: represent opponents fairly and fully
rubrics_metrics.description: Give "merited honour to every one... who has calmness to see and honesty to state what his opponents and their opinions really are, exaggerating nothing to their discredit, keeping nothing back which tells, or can be supposed to tell, in their favour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public debate ought to be governed by frankness and fairness: accurately state opposing views, avoid exaggeration, and disclose favorable points. This is the norm the public should enforce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow freedom of action for experimentation of living and variety of character
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is useful that... there should be different experiments of living; that free scope should be given to varieties of character, short of injury to others; and that the worth of different modes of life should be proved practically."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society should tolerate diverse lifestyles and experiments in living as a way to discover what best promotes human flourishing, provided they do not unjustifiably harm others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal choice and self-directed development exercise and cultivate mental and moral faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Doing things because others do them "calls into no exercise" the faculties; "the faculties are... improved only by being used" — choosing for oneself exercises perception, judgment, discrimination, activity, and self-control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education and social arrangements should enable individuals to make choices for themselves so their faculties develop; blind conformity atrophies judgment and moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desires and impulses are part of a complete human nature and should be cultivated, not uniformly suppressed
rubrics_metrics.description: "Desires and impulses are as much a part of a perfect human being, as beliefs and restraints... Strong impulses are but another name for energy. Energy may be turned to bad uses; but more good may always be made of an energetic nature, than of an indolent and impassive one."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage cultivation and moral guidance of strong impulses rather than suppressing them; balance and moral training are needed rather than prohibition of energetic characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance of conflicting opinions is necessary because even correct doctrines gain vitality only through challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only does suppression risk losing truths, but "the dogma becoming a mere formal profession, inefficacious for good..." — doctrines require challenge to retain meaning and effect on character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public policy and social norms should favor open contestation so even correct doctrines remain rationally grounded and effective; avoid insulating true doctrines from debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law and authority have no business restraining most controversial invective; opinion should judge advocacy's morality
rubrics_metrics.description: While denunciation of invective, sarcasm, personality and the like "would deserve more sympathy if it were ever proposed to interdict them equally to both sides; but it is only desired to restrain the employment of them against the prevailing opinion... law and authority have no business with restraining either, while opinion ought... to determine its verdict by the circumstances of the individual case."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer informal social sanction and moral judgment over legal prohibition for policing abusive rhetoric, because legal restraint tends to be asymmetrical and dangerous to minority expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept some one-sidedness and unjust protests as the price of diversity of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: "The exclusive pretension made by a part of the truth to be the whole, must and ought to be protested against; and if a reactionary impulse should make the protestors unjust in their turn, this one-sidedness, like the other, may be lamented, but must be tolerated."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolerance entails enduring some unfairness and excess on all sides; avoid using such imperfections as a pretext for suppression — the net benefit of diversity justifies tolerating some injustice in advocacy.
